#6693. Spice Up Your Mani with Cinnamon Brown Nails This Fall

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

At this point, we all know that a brown manicure is a fall staple. Even as I type this right now, I’m wearing one that’s a week old (in DND Spiced Brown, if you’re wondering). Espresso nails? Love. Chocolate brown nails? Yep. Chai latte nails? A lighter way to do things. But, it turns out we haven’t exhausted every way to wear the shade quite yet. The latest brown look to get on my radar is cinnamon nails, the warm, spicy take on the fall-friendly color. And honestly, with the holidays around the corner, the smell of cinnamon is sure to be wafting through my kitchen for the next couple months, so the timing couldn’t be better.

These warm, spicy nails combine rich brown with subtle red and copper undertones for a cozy, cinnamon-inspired shade that feels tailor-made for autumn. Ahead, with the help of celebrity nail artist Stephanie Stone (she’s Sally Hansen’s nail style director and has worked with lots of your favorite stars—ahem, Charli XCX) I’ll break down everything you need to know about trending cinnamon brown nails, including plenty of inspo pics, tips for getting the look, and polish recommendations.

As the name suggests, cinnamon brown nails are inspired by the warm, reddish-brown hue of the spice itself. It’s warmer than a classic brown and less red than a terracotta, sitting right in between the two. While espresso and chocolate brown nails tend to lean darker and cooler, these bring some toasty and earthy vibes to your fingertips. While a classic creamy polish looks great in cinnamon, the shade also offers plenty of opportunities to play around with the finish, like with a dimensional velvet cat eye manicure or a chrome topper.

The latter is one of Stone’s favorite ways to wear the trend—she reaches for Sally Hansen’s Miracle Gel in Chics in Charge to get the effect. “Think the glazed donut’s cousin coming to visit for winter break,” she says. And especially apt for the holidays, you can add a little dazzle to the shade: “If you want to give them some extra sparkle, add a crystal at the base of your nails for an extra catch of light,” she adds.

Stone puts it perfectly: “Every great manicure starts with immaculate cuticle prep and nail care.” Before reaching for any polish, “trim and file your nails to their desired shape,” she says. “Then use Sally Hansen’s Push & Buff Cuticle Pen to clean your nail plate of an excess dead skin.” This helps clean up your cuticles easily and quickly. Next, “wash your hands with soap and water and wipe your nail beds with alcohol,” she adds, noting how important this final prep step is, especially if you’re doing a metallic finish. “Metallic shimmer and polishes expose any texture or dust you may have on your nails,” she explains.

Then, it’s polish time. This part is pretty straightforward: Paint your nails with two coats of your favorite beige or brown nail polish, she says, recommending a medium brown shade “if you want your nail look to be reminiscent of a cinnamon roll” or a reddish brown “if you want your nails more reminiscent of cinnamon as the spice itself.” After letting dry for a few minutes, add top coat and cuticle oil to finish things off. Need some product recs? Stone’s go-to polish is Sally Hansen’s Miracle Gel Polish in Been There, Dune That, but you can also get the look with Olive & June’s Nail Polish in Sassy Molasses or Essie’s Gel Couture Liquid Diamonds in Marquise Please too.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmo. She’s covered and tested all things nails, from the coolest new polish colors to cuticle care and nail art trends.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmopolitan and was previously the beauty assistant at Good Housekeeping, Woman's Day, and Prevention.

#6691. Rosalía Wins With Her Style at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards

She wore a quartet of designer looks from Matières Fécales, Erdem, Vivienne Westwood, and Dior

Rosalía won big at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards last night. For her fourth studio album, Lux, the Spanish pop singer took home her third trophy for Album of the Year, becoming the first woman in the history of the ceremony to ever do so. She collected a total of five awards, coming out on top in other major categories like Song of the Year, which was awarded to her track “La Perla” (featuring Yahritza y Su Esencia), and Best Short Form Music Video, which went to her visual for “Sauvignon Blanc.” And to coincide with such a major night, Rosalía brought out a few major designer looks, all styled by Chloe & Chenelle Delgadillo.

To start the evening, the “Berghain” singer hit the red carpet in the avant-garde label of the moment, Matières Fécales, which has been embraced by everyone from Zendaya to Rihanna and Demi Moore.

Courtesy of the label’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection, Rosalía’s angelic white gown featured a ruched tulle bodice with semi-sheer folds that hugged her body and culminated in the house’s signature déchiré detailing. The tattered fragments arched from Rosalía’s shoulders like wings, while also dangling from the ends of her cropped sleeves. Down low, there was equal drama courtesy of a dramatic tulle bubble skirt that trailed around her in a voluminous cascade. Of course, her signature halo-dyed hair acted as the perfect complement to the heavenly ensemble.

Later, Rosalía hit the stage to perform a medley of songs from Lux, including “La Perla,” “La Rumba del Perdón,” and “Dios Es un Stalker.” For her performance, she wore a bespoke satin gown from Erdem, pulled from the house’s Fall/Winter 2026 collection. (Just last month, she turned to the same London-based label for a stunning balletcore street-style moment.)

The golden-hued design featured a corset-style bodice and knotted bows along the neckline, with a basque waist and flared ruffle skirt that was overlayed with black tulle and trimmed with ostrich feathers.

Once she returned to her seat, it turned out Rosalía had another surprise look in store, as she changed into a custom white dress from Vivienne Westwood. The bridal-inspired design featured a strapless, plunging sweetheart bodice decorated with a tiny bow in the middle, while layers of fabric were draped along the waist for a subtle peplum effect.

All of the fabric, meanwhile, was embroidered with floral lace details and microscopic pearl embellishments, and the singer wore a scarf to match, while slipping into a pair of contrasting black pumps.

To finish her quartet of looks, Rosalía switched into a custom black Dior dress by Jonathan Anderson, who, fittingly, also helped design many of the looks for the Spanish superstar’s recent Lux Tour.

The silky black slip featured two delicate lace straps that hung off Rosalía’s shoulders, while the bust tied into a knot that dangled in front like a tassel. The top half of the dress was decorated with subtle floral details, while the skirt featured panels of semi-sheer material. It all worked perfectly to serve as an inky backdrop as Rosalía posed with her stack of gramophone trophies.

As she accepted her prize for Album of the Year, Rosalía got teary-eyed, saying: “This is the third time I’ve won this award. If El Mal Querer was a dream, and Motomami was a bold gamble, then Lux has been a leap into the unknown. I believe it’s very important to speak your own truth—and for others to be able to speak theirs—and this record is mine. I thank God, and I thank my loved ones: my family and my friends. Thank you for your love and for shaping me into who I am today. The truth is, I know I still have a lot to learn, and I’m certain that I likely haven’t even created my best work yet.”

#6689. Ana de Armas’s Complete Dating History

From Ben Affleck to Tom Cruise and beyond.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Ana de Armas has experienced a stratospheric rise in Hollywood over the past decade. 2015’s Knock Knock—a thriller starring Keanu Reeves—provided the Cuban, American, and Spanish actress with her stateside breakout role. Since then, de Armas has appeared in numerous box office and critical hits, such as 2017’s Blade Runner 2049, 2019’s Knives Out, 2021’s No Time to Die, 2022’s Blonde, and 2025’s John Wick spin-off Ballerina.

Offscreen, the actress has had several public romances, too. Most recently, she has been linked to Venezuelan singer Beto Montenegro, with the pair photographed kissing during a summer getaway in Spain. In November 2026, they made their first red carpet appearance together at the Latin Recording Academy’s Person of the Year Gala in Las Vegas.

Here’s what you need to know about Ana de Armas’s dating history.

Prior to making it big as a Hollywood actress, de Armas relocated from Havana to Spain, where she met her first husband, Marc Clotet. The Ghosted star began dating the Spanish model and actor in 2010, with the pair marrying the following year in July 2011, Hola! magazine reported.

Unfortunately, the couple’s marriage didn’t last. During an appearance at the 27th Goya Awards in Spain on Feb. 17, 2013, Clotet revealed, “Yes, we’ve broken up. It was by mutual agreement. I’m calm.” According to Diez Minutos, Clotet also shared that he and de Armas were “still friends” despite the split.

According to La Razón, de Armas started dating Spanish screenwriter and director David Victori in August 2013. The publication also noted that the couple lived together in Los Angeles, but had returned to Spain in March 2014 for the Málaga Film Festival. Although it’s unclear when Victori and de Armas ended their relationship, it’s been reported that they split sometime in 2014.

Following her breakups from Clotet and Victori, de Armas decided to move to Los Angeles full time to further her career, telling The Hollywood Reporter, “I don’t like feeling stuck, like I’m not going anywhere. I wanted more.”

After permanently relocating to America, de Armas began “a serious relationship with agent Franklin Latt,” Vanity Fair reported. During her interview with the publication, the War Dogs actress was quick to dispel the idea that dating a successful Hollywood agent—Latt now manages Pedro Pascal at Creative Artists Agency—aided her career in any way. “For anyone who ever questions...how did I get to do this or that, fuck them,” she said. “They will not get to spend their New Year’s with me. They are not the people whose opinion I should care about. They are not the people I share my happiness with.”

In 2017, de Armas started dating artist Alejandro Piñeiro Bello, who was also born in Havana. During their relationship, the pair regularly posted photos of one another on social media, which have since been deleted from their respective accounts.

In February 2018, de Armas marked the launch of Piñeiro Bello’s pop-up exhibition in Los Angeles by writing on Instagram, “So proud of you,” and he returned the favor, thanking the actress for all of her “hard work and love,” according to Antena 3.

Porter later confirmed that de Armas had split from Piñeiro Bello in 2019 after two years of dating.

After meeting on the set of thriller Deep Water in late 2019, de Armas started a very public relationship with Ben Affleck. In March 2020, a source told People that the pair had “great chemistry right from the start,” but “there were no signs of romance” until filming had wrapped. In a March 2020 interview with Vogue Spain (translated by People), de Armas discussed working with the Oscar winner, saying, “His talent is infinite.” The same month, de Armas made her relationship with Affleck official when she shared photos of him on Instagram.

Affleck and de Armas were regularly photographed walking their dogs together in Los Angeles, where the couple quarantined together during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

In June 2020, de Armas and Affleck attended a Black Lives Matter march together, per People. Following a double date with Affleck’s best friend, Matt Damon, and his wife, People reported that de Armas officially moved into her boyfriend’s property in August 2020. “She’s aware that his family comes first,” a source told the outlet. “And appreciates that. They work very hard at that balance.” For Affleck’s 48th birthday, the Overdrive actress gave her beau a custom-built BMW motorcycle, according to People.

In November 2020, the pair traveled to New Orleans for reshoots of their movie Deep Water. As de Armas appeared to be wearing a diamond ring in photos from the set, rumors started to swirl regarding a possible engagement. However, according to People, the jewelry item was simply a prop for the film. The very same month, de Armas and Affleck spent their first Thanksgiving together, along with the actor’s three children—Violet, Fin, and Samuel—whom he shares with ex-wife Jennifer Garner, E! News reported.

Unfortunately, by January 2021, de Armas and Affleck had called it quits. “Ben is no longer dating Ana,” a source told People. “She broke it off. Their relationship was complicated. Ana doesn’t want to be Los Angeles-based and Ben obviously has to since his kids live in Los Angeles.” People reported that the breakup occurred “over the phone.” Soon after the split, Affleck reconnected with his ex Jennifer Lopez.

Following her split from Affleck, de Armas was romantically linked to Tinder executive Paul Boukadakis in June 2021. In December 2021, an insider told E! News that the couple’s romance was “very serious.”

A July 2022 profile of de Armas in ELLE revealed that she met her new boyfriend “during the pandemic through a mutual friend.” With the majority of bars and restaurants closed during lockdown, they “spent their first dates at each other’s homes, drinking wine and talking.”

As for how she spent her 34th birthday in April 2022, de Armas told ELLE that she celebrated with “my man, my dogs, Chris [Evans] and the crew [of Ghosted].” She continued, “I wasn’t home having a romantic dinner; I was on set with my people doing what I love and at the beach and having a shot of Fireball...and it is the happiest I’ve been.”

The pair was pictured arriving at the Venice Film Festival in September 2022, and they posed for photos on the red carpet at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party on March 12, 2023. While it’s unclear when de Armas and Boukadakis ended their romance, People reported the split in November 2024, when the actress was spotted kissing another man.

The Exposed star surprised fans when she started dating Manuel Anido Cuesta, the stepson of Cuba’s president, Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez. Having graduated with a law degree from the University of Havana in 2019, Anido Cuesta reportedly “became part of the Cuban regime’s inner circle,” La Nación reported. The outlet further explained, “Although he does not hold official positions in government institutions, he has been seen at numerous events and on official trips accompanying his stepfather and mother.”

Rumors began circulating about a potential romance between de Armas and Anido Cuesta in May 2024, when a Cuban influencer claimed the pair had spent 10 days together on the island of Cayo Santa María, off the north coast of Cuba, per Periódico Cubano. While the majority of de Armas’s romance with Anido Cuesta remained private, Hola! published photographs of the pair kissing one another during a night out in Madrid in November 2024. Breakup reports ultimately surfaced in May 2025.

Mission: Impossible icon Tom Cruise and de Armas first sparked dating rumors in winter 2025. The two actors had been spending time together due to work.

While promoting her John Wick spin-off Ballerina in June 2025, de Armas commented on her connection with Cruise, telling Variety, “We’re working together, so he got to see Ballerina and he actually really liked it.” She continued, “It is very special that someone like him is supporting [Ballerina].”

In mid-July 2025, a source downplayed the romance rumors, telling People that de Armas and Cruise simply had “a special work relationship.” According to the insider, the pair had been spending extended periods of time together while preparing to co-star in the thriller Deeper, from the director of 2005’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith, Doug Liman. “Tom is an incredible mentor to Ana,” the source alleged. “She has nothing but amazing things to say about him.”

The end of July brought two eyebrow-raising outings for de Armas and Cruise. On July 26, the pair made an unexpected cameo at an Oasis concert in London, appearing in the background of an Instagram video shared by music producer Goldie. The following day, de Armas and Cruise materialized in Vermont, where they were photographed holding hands, eating ice cream, and shopping together.

In October 2025, People reported that de Armas and Cruise were only ever friends. A source said Cruise was a “dear friend and mentor” to her and added, “She’s single, though, and has been for a while. She stays in touch with Tom and they still have an upcoming movie project that she’s looking forward to.”

De Armas sparked romance rumors with Venezuelan singer Beto Montenegro in summer 2026. The pair was seen together at a concert in Madrid, where Hola! captured a video of them dancing on July 29.

The speculation intensified in August when de Armas and Montenegro traveled to Formentera, Spain. On August 2, they were photographed holding hands and kissing while making their way to the beach.

On November 11, de Armas and Montenegro made their red carpet debut together at the Latin Recording Academy’s 2026 Person of the Year Gala in Las Vegas.

The actress wore a black Wiederhoeft look featuring a corseted top and sheer lace skirt, while Montenegro opted for a black suit with a light blue shirt and dark tie.

#6688. Jennifer Lawrence Swaps Her Pops of Lemon for a Polished Dark Monochrome Look

Complete with a glossy Hermès crocodile Kelly

Jennifer Lawrence can just as easily pull off a bright lemon-yellow Colleen Allen coat or a pair of funky sequined pink Siedrés pants as she can a polished, monochromatic business look.

Earlier this week, the actor looked so chic in an outfit composed of timeless navy and black staples. The base of her look was made up of an elongated, buttoned blazer, and matching trousers. To continue the color scheme, she wrapped a navy scarf around her neck.

Then came the luxurious black accents: square sunglasses and a rare Hermès Kelly Sellier in shiny crocodile leather and gold hardware. And because Lawrence cannot live without her pops of color, the actor slipped on a pair of burgundy velvet slippers.

Lawrence is often one to go minimalist with her jewelry and glam, and she did that here, opting for polish-free nails, minimal makeup, and a few gold rings (one of them being her engagement ring from husband Cooke Maroney).

As you may have guessed, the cherry on top of the look was Lawrence’s dirty-blonde hair, which was styled down in easy, breezy long waves. The Hunger Games alum recently introduced her haircare brand, Mes, and has since been promoting her products around town.

“I feel like if my hair looks good, no one will notice anything else about my face, my clothes, or my body,” the actor joked in a recent interview with The Cut.

Of course, we disagree. While we do love a good hair day, we’ll never miss a J.Law street-style moment.

#6687. ‘DWTS’ Frontrunner Amber Glenn Has Had to Make a Major Decision to Stay in the Competition

Competing for the Mirrorball means making some tough choices off the dance floor.

We all know Amber Glenn is a fierce competitor, thanks to her Olympic gold medals. So, it’s no surprise she’s one of the semifinalists on Dancing With the Stars season 35. But what fans might not know is how much she’s given up to keep pushing toward the Mirrorball trophy.

According to The Sun, Amber has stepped back from figure skating events to focus on the beloved reality competition. She was most recently removed from the entry list for the NHK Trophy in Japan, which kicks off later this month. It’s the sixth and final event in the Grand Prix regular season and the second figure skating event she’s opted out of at the last minute.

Amber also withdrew from this week’s Saatva Skate America competition in Everett, Washington, as she preps for the DWTS semifinals.

“For now, Amber is focused solely on DWTS, which has taken up most of her energy and time with grueling rehearsals and weekly live shows,” the outlet reports.

The Olympian is a frontrunner for this year’s coveted prize, up against Maura Higgins, Connor Wood, Harry Shum Jr., Ezra Frech, and Tatyana Ali.

During a November 12 appearance on The Zach Sang Show, Amber opened up about what it would mean for her to help her pro partner, Pasha Pashkov, win his first-ever Mirrorball trophy.

“That would mean the world because, and I’ve said this before, is that I came into this competition like, of course, who doesn’t want to win?” she said. “But it wasn’t like, ‘I need this because I’ve worked my entire life for it.’ Like, I’ve been dancing for two months. Yes, it has been a very intense, very passionate two months of working, but it has been his whole life that he has been dancing.”

She continued, “Imagine how much work I’m putting into it. He’s doing twice that amount because he has to choreograph. He has to do so many, like, visual selections. Like, there’s so much that the pro does for every single show that people don’t see.So yes, it’s about the celeb and who wins, but it also is about the pro.”

Though Amber has had to give up some skating for ballroom dancing, there’s a chance she’ll be back on the ice at the Prevagen U.S. Championships later this season in January.

In the meantime, we can’t wait to see her crush the DWTS semifinals next week!

#6686. I Found the Most Comfortable Pointed-Toe Boots

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Buying pointed-toe boots has always been a challenge for me because I’m built like a ballerina—not, sadly, in terms of long legs or elegant arms or a swanlike neck, but in terms of feet. I have the bunions of a woman who has dedicated her life to the art of dance, which is ironic because I took ballet lessons for all of three months when I was eight. (I quit after they let me wear the tutu, which was really the only thing I was in it for.) I am confessing this not because I enjoy talking about my feet on the internet, but to establish my credibility when I say that I have finally found a pair of slim, sexy, pointed-toe boots that are comfortable enough to wear all day, even for those of us with less-than-ideal extremities.

Margaux’s Inga boots have a long, squared-off toe and a little kitten heel that measures 1.5 inches—tall enough to give you a bit of a lift, but low enough to be walkable. They come in black leather and a sleek espresso suede, both of which look great with jeans but would also be cute peeking out of long, drapey trousers. The best part is the sizing: Margaux offers its boots in narrow, medium, and wide, and somehow, through the magic of proportion play, the wide does not look wide. They accommodate the fullest part of my foot without looking bulky or breaking up the nice long line.

The first time I wore them, it was to a witches’ dinner that my friend Mo throws every Halloween. She invites 30 of her best female friends over, decorates her home in high goth style, and serves us a theatrically witchy meal. (This time, it was black squid-ink pasta.) Of course, one has to dress appropriately to dine with the coven, so I paired the boots with slim black jeans and a sheer black polka-dotted top. Not only did I get a bunch of compliments, but I didn’t find myself pining for my broomstick on the walk home—the boots were just as comfortable at the end of the evening as they’d been at the start of the night.

They’ve held up equally well on the commute to work. In addition to the extra width, they also come with five millimeters of cushioning on the inside, which is enough to protect you when you’re pounding the pavement. Ever since slimmer toes reentered the fashion conversation, I’ve been faced with the choice between sitting out the trend or hobbling around in boots that fundamentally do not fit. As much as I love a good pair of shoes, I also live for a long walk, and the Ingas, miraculously, let me have both. Really, they don’t feel like heels at all, which is a rare and wonderful thing for a pair of pointed-toe kitten-heel boots.

#6684. How to Layer Clothes for Fall and Winter Without Sacrificing Style

Fall is officially here and I am doing everything to stay warm. Layering is a very necessary skill come the colder months of the year. Not only is it practical—keeping you warm and such—but it also makes your fall and winter outfits that much more interesting.

As a Florida native now in the Northeast, layering is something I’m just now getting the hang of. And if you’re like me, either new to the cold or been here for years and can’t quite get it, I’ve got you covered. Below, I’ve gathered a few fall layering styling tips so you can lean into the fun of it all.

One of my favorite cozy pieces in my closet is an oversized turtleneck sweater. Not only will it keep you warm, but it is very chic. A fun way to elevate what could be seen as a simple look is tying your sweater around your waist, but specifically off to the side. It adds an undeniable touch of cool.

When first getting into layering, you can always start small. And doubling up on your shirts is the easiest way to achieve warmth. Raise the stakes by showing off those layers, either by wearing a longer shirt underneath or slightly raising the top shirt so the one underneath is visible. Even more points if the shirts are different colors so you get a color-blocking moment. Add in a peekaboo jacket zipped similarly to the look above and you’re set.

Belt layering is definitely more for the styling side of fall/winter layering, but it’s just as important. When trying to bring a little more life to a cold weather look, belt stacking is a fashion-forward option I personally love.

Oversized jackets are the real winners of fall. Especially a leather jacket like the one above. Add in a patterned sweater tied around the waist for a little more fun and you’ve got a perfect look.

Similar to tying around the waist, adding a scarf over top of your coat is another more style-forward layering tip that might not necessarily provide all the warmth, but brings the style.

A true Y2K favorite of mine that works great for the colder months is dresses over jeans. If you’re into nostalgia fashion, this is a more modern way to tap into the trend, while also staying warm.

#6683. Denis Villeneuve Talks ‘Dune: Part Three’ and Rebooting James Bond: ‘We Cannot F*ck It Up.’

“I’m out of a job,” Denis Villeneuve said, jokingly. Hours earlier, Villeneuve had signed off on the IMAX 70-milimeter print of Dune: Part Three, officially wrapping post-production on that film—and in turn, a decade-long chapter of the Quebecois writer-director’s working life.

Fresh off this milestone, Villeneuve and GQ had come to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles for a conversation and a private screening of Dune: Part Two, presented by OMEGA, in honor of his anointment as GQ’s Director of the Year. Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi introduced Villeneuve before the director and GQ’s Zach Baron dove into a conversation that covered his original Dune plans, where Dune: Part Three breaks from its predecessors, and Villeneuve’s feelings about taking over the James Bond franchise.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi and Zach Baron with Denis Villeneuve

“I feel light,” the director of the year told Baron, then added, “Numb.” He was still processing Dune’s end, he said—while also coming to grips with closing the book on “the most rewarding, inspiring, and best ten years of my life as a filmmaker.”

Villeneuve’s first two Dune films have raked in more than a billion dollars at the box office. Part Three appears likely to nearly double that when it hits theaters (and locks up most of the world’s IMAX screens) a week before Christmas. But at one point during his conversation with Baron, the director pushed back gently on the notion of these movies as a “franchise.”

“There was nothing industrial in the way they were made,” Villeneuve said. They were the work of “a bunch of friends”—a familial crew, out in the desert putting things together.

“In French,” the Quebecois director continued, “there is a word—artisanal. They are very personal. Made with a lot of care. They’re little big things—but in a way, they are delicate.”

After all, as sprawling and cosmically grand as they are, these movies are also a deeply personal project for the director, born of images that took root in his head when he first read Frank Herbert’s thick-as-a-brick, notoriously adaptation-resistant 1965 novel Dune at age 13. Later, as Villeneuve racked up credits and clout, people would ask him what his dream project was; the answer was always Dune.

“I kept saying to myself, Someone else will do it one day,” he told Baron. “Another filmmaker will adapt this book again. And I kept waiting, and I kept waiting, until I felt ready to do it myself.”

Herbert wrote five escalatingly bonkers Dune sequels before his death in 1986, but Villeneuve intended to walk away from the table after adapting the first book across two films.

“Trilogies are very dangerous,” he told Baron. “The first movie is a promise, and if you fulfill the promise with the second one, then there’s a feeling of security that comes with that, and you feel that you have a recipe…That’s the trap. Because then you repeat yourself.”

But after wrapping Part Two, Villeneuve found himself unable to stop thinking about Dune Messiah—the second Dune novel, which Herbert supposedly wrote in frustration, believing the audience had missed the point by embracing Paul Atreides as a hero.

Villeneuve said his take on Messiah is “a different beast” than the first two films, built it around the tension between Timothée Chalamet’s Paul and his Fremen consort Chani (Zendaya), who Villeneuve has re-imagined—in a pivotal departure from Herbert’s version—as a nonbeliever who takes a critical view of Paul’s rise to power.

Neel Shah, Timothy Simons, and Michael Lasker

Of course, the specter (S.P.E.C.T.R.E.?) of another franchise hung over the proceedings at the Lucas Museum. Villeneuve, after all, is only technically between jobs; he’s a self-described “monomaniac” who insists that he can only hyper-focus on one project at a time and has been locked in on Dune for a decade, but the as-yet-untitled 26th Bond film is in motion, with Villeneuve signed on to direct.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi, Denis Villeneuve, and OMEGA’s Lucien Jornod

He could say almost nothing in public about the project, or even when he’d begin shooting it—he joked about having “the target of the sniper” on his chest—but spoke of feeling the responsibility not to fail: “We cannot fuck it up. We do not have the choice.”

Over the past week, the casting rumors around Villeneuve’s Bond reboot have reached what our UK colleagues accurately termed the “fever-dream” stage. It might be Callum Turner or Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, but it might be Robert Pattinson, who’s emerged as a surprise front-runner after months of supposition about the part being earmarked for a relative unknown. At some point, toward the end of Tuesday’s conversation, the subject of Bond 26’s lead could no longer be avoided.

“Has the role of James Bond been cast?” Baron asked the director.

“It’s—it’s in the process. In the process,” Villeneuve said with a smile. “I am pushing the gas.”

“Blink once for Robert Pattinson,” Baron suggested, “and twice for Callum Turner.”

Villeneuve, for the record, did not blink. ✦

GQ would like to thank Legendary Entertainment, Warner Bros., and Brianna Smith.

#6682. Rosalía Co-Signs One of This Year’s Most Viral Looks at the Latin Grammys

Rosalía is having a heavenly year, and she has the wardrobe to match. At last night’s Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas, the Spanish superstar, who took home a suite of awards including Album of the Year for Lux and Song of the Year for “La Perla,” delivered a series of fantastical, sent-from-above fashion moments.

First up? A gloriously frothy white creation from Matières Fécales, one of the year’s most talked-about—and increasingly celebrity-beloved—fashion labels. Styled by Chloe and Chenelle, Rosalía arrived in a custom gown inspired by the Paris-based label’s spring 2027 collection. The look featured a sheer, tightly ruched corset bodice, clouds of tulle billowing around the shoulders, and an enormous, floor-sweeping skirt. It compounded much of the star’s ongoing aesthetic, which oscillates between bridal confection, prima ballerina, and celestial apparition. Right at home in the spiritually charged universe of Lux.

Matières Fécales, the provocative label founded by Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran, has quickly become something of a red-carpet phenomenon. Lady Gaga brought its gothic sensibilities to the Grammys earlier this year in a dramatic black feathered gown; Zendaya wore a winged, goddess-like white creation to The Odyssey premiere, and a frayed salmon-pink gown while promoting The Drama. Demi Moore embraced its more extravagant side in a hot-pink Cannes ballgown, while Sarah Paulson and María Zardoya both chose the label for the 2026 Met Gala. There’s a mesmerizing balance of the grotesque and the gorgeous, with shredded fabrics and surreal proportions that coexist with sweeping, exquisitely feminine silhouettes. Rosalía, naturally, is game.

The look fits into the singer’s ever-ambitious fashion vocabulary. Her Lux era has seen her fully embrace the possibilities of fashion as performance, spanning everything from religious iconography to the delicate discipline of ballet. For her tour, Jonathan Anderson created a suite of extraordinary custom Dior costumes, including an embellished organza tutu, a pale-blue pannier dress, a militaristic ensemble with a tricorne hat, and an angel-wing cape. Another heavenly look came courtesy of Argentinian designer Sofía Abadi; Rosalía stepped out wearing her stand-out signature Angel jacket, with its hand-knitted cascade of interlocking and braided cream woolen fringe to create a winged effect. Ballet has also spilled into her off-duty wardrobe: recall the latex-and-tulle tutu dress by emerging designer Yasmina Atta, or her towering archival Junko Shimada ballet platforms.

And what makes Rosalía’s style so exciting is her willingness to champion both the established and the experimental. Alongside the grand maisons, she’s worn emerging names like Monique Fei, Rosalie Bernard, the aforementioned Abadi, and Laura Andraschko, while also indulging in archival McQueen and Nicolas Ghesquière-era Balenciaga. While adventurous, she retains an elegance and ethereality.

The Matières Fécales gown was only the beginning. For her opening performance, Rosalía changed into a custom Erdem gown in a rich, shimmering chartreuse-gold—one of fashion’s most irresistible colors of the moment—with a structured corset, romantic off-the-shoulder bows, and a full, gathered skirt. Later, she returned to the stage to accept her awards wearing ivory Vivienne Westwood Couture: a lace, corseted gown with a delicate high-neck collar and an asymmetric skirt. She closed the evening in a black satin Dior slip dress by Jonathan Anderson, posing and beaming with her awards. Felicidades!

#6679. Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez’s Full Relationship Timeline

Nearly a decade after ending their relationship, Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez are back in the public eye.

The former couple recently sparked reconciliation rumors after they were spotted spending time together in Texas and Florida during Grande’s Eternal Sunshine Tour. Grande also made multiple changes to the Ricky lyric in “Thank U, Next,” prompting fans to wonder whether the pair had rekindled their romance.

On July 14, People confirmed that they were back on—but taking things slowly. “Ariana has always considered Ricky a friend,” a source told People. “She’s not held ill will against him [since their split]. Ricky is dependable, trustworthy and very supportive. Ariana feels she can be herself around Ricky.”

Grande and Alvarez first met when he joined her as a backup dancer on her 2015 Honeymoon Tour. They dated for about a year before separating in 2016, but have maintained a friendly relationship ever since.

Below, a full timeline of everything we know about Ariana Grande and Ricky Alvarez’s relationship.

Grande and Alvarez met while he worked as a backup dancer on her Honeymoon Tour. They began dating that year.

Grande briefly spoke about their relationship in a Billboard cover story.

“We’re happy,” she said. “I’m a very happy girl. I have a healthy life right now, and I think that’s all anyone cares to know. The end.”

The story also included comments from Grande’s friend Victoria Monét, who shared that “Moonlight” was inspired by the beginning of Grande and Alvarez’s relationship.

“That’s what Ricky called her one night,” Monét said. “I think it was after their first kiss. He waited to kiss her for a long time, and she was really impressed. He’s such a gentleman, and the song is a great little bookmark of the start of their relationship.”

Multiple outlets reported that Grande and Alvarez had ended their relationship after about a year together.

Grande referenced Alvarez in her hit single “Thank U, Next,” singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / Now I listen and laugh.”

After the song’s release, Alvarez shared videos of himself reacting to the lyric on Instagram Stories.

“Nothing but gratitude,” he wrote. “Thank you, next… (those songs are fire tho… you’re welcome).”

Grande reposted his Stories and joked about the lyric herself.

“HAHAHAHAHHAHAHAH IM SORRY U GOT THE WORST LINE. It was meant v lovingly.”

When fans later speculated that the pair had reunited after they interacted on Instagram, Grande shut down the rumors herself in the comments of one of Alvarez’s posts.

“We’re friends, everyone take a big ol breather,” she wrote.

Years later, Grande and Alvarez were photographed together in Austin, Texas, ahead of one of her Eternal Sunshine Tour stops. Photos circulating online showed them dining with a group while Grande celebrated her birthday in the city.

According to TMZ, sources familiar with the situation said Alvarez was one of several friends spending time with Grande and that the outing was purely platonic. People also reported that the pair had “been hanging out recently.”

During her Austin concerts, Grande also made noticeable changes to the Ricky lyric in “Thank U, Next.”

Earlier in the week, she sang, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / And they still kinda slap.” At another performance, she changed the line again, singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / I know he’s still got my back.”

Over Fourth of July weekend, Grande and Alvarez were photographed shopping together at a Whole Foods in Boca Raton, Florida, before heading to celebrate the holiday with Grande’s family, according to TMZ.

The outing came after Grande wrapped three sold-out Eternal Sunshine Tour shows in nearby Sunrise.

The following day, People published additional details about their friendship, citing a source who said Alvarez has been joining Grande for portions of her tour.

“She’s having a great time on tour. She loves having close friends join her for parts of the tour,” the source said. “Ricky has always been a friend and confidant. She really trusts him. He has such great, positive energy, makes her laugh, and she enjoys spending time with him.”

The source also addressed Grande’s life following her breakup from Ethan Slater.

“Her relationship with Ethan is 100 percent over. She’s focused on her tour and spending time with the people who have always been there for her,” the source said. “Ariana is having the best time reconnecting with fans and loves being onstage.”

Grande fueled reconciliation rumors herself a week later on July 13. She changed the Ricky lyric of “Thank U, Next” again during her Brooklyn show, singing, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / We always find our way back.”

Hours later on July 14, sources confirmed to People and TMZ that they were officially dating again. The insiders told both outlets that they were taking things very slowly.

“They’re not jumping into anything serious right away, but Ari is happy to have him back in her life,” a source told People. The insider added that they “have a similar, smart, dry sense of humor.”

On July 16, Grande and Alvarez were photographed walking in Central Park with their arms wrapped around each other. It marked their first public sighting since news of their reconciliation broke.

On July 17, TMZ shared more pictures of the couple enjoying some PDA from the same day. In the images, Alvarez is embracing Grande as she leans toward him on the street.

Alvarez went out and supported Grande while she performed in Brooklyn. The dancer was spotted at her July 18 and 19 Eternal Sunshine Tour shows. On the second night, he and Grande’s brother, Frankie Grande, had a sweet moment.

On July 27, Grande soft-launched her relationship with Alvarez on Instagram. The singer tagged him in a Polaroid of herself, seemingly giving him credit for taking it.

On August 12, Grande went Instagram official with Alvarez, sharing two photos of them together in a carousel post. “🌱 ！ ♡,” she captioned it.

Days after Grande made her relationship with Alvarez Instagram official, fans noticed that the couple appears to share a meaningful tattoo. During the London stop of her Eternal Sunshine Tour, Grande displayed a new piece across her upper chest reading, “I do love you.” Alvarez has the same phrase tattooed near his collarbone, though his version appears in a different typeface.

A few days later, they were seen in London, where Grande was set to start her 10-day residency. The couple was wearing two cozy layered looks in the cooler U.K. temperatures, with Grande wearing an oversize white cardigan and Alvarez in a jean jacket. They walked arm-in-arm down the street, immersed in conversation.

Grande and Alvarez were also photographed out in London with Grande’s mom, Joan, on August 27. In the photos, Grande and Alvarez walked hand-in-hand as they made their way through the city.

Grande wore a fitted white graphic T-shirt with dark-wash jeans, oversize sunglasses, and a white headband, while Alvarez kept things casual in a white T-shirt, jeans, and a baseball cap. Joan joined them in an all-black look with pink earrings.

During the final show of her Eternal Sunshine Tour at London’s O2 Arena, Grande gave Alvarez another shout-out while performing “Thank U, Next.”

When she reached the lyric about her boyfriend, she changed the original line to, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / I’m tryna make him my last.”

That same week, Alvarez shared his photos from Grande’s tour, including one of her kissing his hand in what appears to be a dressing room. He otherwise captured her in motion, performing onstage.

“It’s the best thing to do,” he wrote in the caption.

The post comes shortly after Grande shared a snippet of them kissing at her rehearsals in London. The intimate moment was part of a video montage she shared at the end of her Eternal Sunshine Tour to thank everyone for what she calls “one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences” of her life.

On November 7, Grande shared an Instagram Reel with Alvarez as the couple played a kissing challenge game for her makeup brand, R.E.M. Beauty.

In the video, Grande sat on Alvarez’s lap while he wore a beanie over his eyes and attempted to guess what lip product she was wearing when she kissed him.

“This is a challenge called ‘What’s on my lips?’” Grande explained.

“Or what’s on my girlfriend’s lips, really,” Alvarez quipped.

The dancer correctly identified several products, including an unreleased shade called Holiday Mélange.

A few days later, on November 11, Alvarez and Grande made their red carpet debut at the New York City premiere of Focker-In-Law.

Grande chose a vintage Badgley Mischka gown with a fitted bodice and full plaid skirt, while Alvarez wore a black blazer over a white shirt with dark jeans.

#6678. Inside the First Competition Between Historic Vintage Timepieces

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

In the automotive world, high-end cars have gone head-to-head since the early 1920s. Judges didn’t evaluate them based on their speed, though—in a Concours d’Élégance, the prize goes to the best-looking vehicles. The tradition continues today in picturesque sites around the world where collectors submit their often very high-end vintage, classic cars. Surprisingly, there has never been an event for vintage timepieces.

Aurel Bacs, the famous auctioneer whose longstanding association with Phillips has shaped the watch collecting world, endeavored to change that. “It began with a meeting where I said, ‘I have a dream,’” he said in a press release. For the very first iteration of this competition, Bacs and Phillips partnered with Swiss heavyweight Vacheron Constantin. They expected to receive maybe 100 to 200 submissions, but the jury was forced to whittle down 550 of them to 34 finalist watches, whose owners were flown out from across the world for the Concours held at the Hôtel Président in Geneva.

“It was the most beautiful evening in the field ever,” Bacs said. At the Hôtel Président, around 200 attendees gathered, along with a jury of 14 watch-industry experts including Bacs himself, Ben Clymer of Hodinkee, writer and historian Nick Foulkes, longtime watch journalist Roberta Naas, and others. Watches could only be submitted for consideration in one category (Chronographs, Métiers d’Art, Chronomètre Royal, Astronomical Complications, Multiple Complications, Design, and Chiming Mechanisms) and were judged based on nine criteria: authenticity, elegance, rarity, impact on the history of Vacheron Constantin and/or on watchmaking in general, provenance, technicality, métiers d’art (artistic crafts), state of preservation, and emotional dimension.

The jurors deliberated over several hours until the winners of the seven categories and a Best of Show were finally selected. Following a cocktail reception, everyone gathered on the lower floor of the Hôtel Président to see the results from the watch world’s first Concours d'Élégance.

The first category featured a smattering of some of the maison’s most important wristwatches, including a highly rare ref. 4072 in stainless steel from 1940. However, it was a yellow gold pocket-watch chronograph from 1929 that won the day. The result was such a surprise that the audience, intimately familiar with the historical importance of pocket watches, audibly gasped inside the room. It made me wonder if these old-fashioned timepieces could regain their lost position as the pinnacle of watch collecting. This piece certainly warranted the love it received: in excellent condition and featuring a white enamel dial with dual registers in an “up-down” configuration, it’s a beautiful timepiece.

This category celebrates handcrafts such as enameling and gem-setting, and it featured a smattering of truly spectacular pieces—mostly sub-40mm wristwatches in precious metals with wild cloisonné or Grand Feu champlevé enamel dials depicting landmasses or animals.

However, a stunning pocket watch set with blue sapphires throughout the bezel and Roman indices won out.

When an older American gentleman stepped on stage to collect his prize, he explained to a stunned crowd that not only had his great-grandfather, Dr. Otto von Frangeš, been given the watch by His Majesty Alexander I of Yugoslavia, its original owner, but that he wore it while sitting in the motorcade during the king’s assassination in France in 1934. Otto’s middle son, Nikola, eventually smuggled the watch out of Yugoslavia by sewing it into the lining of his wife’s jacket as they fled the Iron Curtain in the late 1940s.

In 1907, Vacheron launched the Chronomètre Royal sub-brand, specifically built to endure a life sailing the seas. The model’s parts were anti-magnetic and resisted rusting. The dials were made out of enamel, which could also stand up to the moist atmosphere without rusting. Because they were critical to maritime navigation, timing precision was of the utmost importance, and models from this line frequently won observatory trials (which tested for a watch’s accuracy) that ran from the 1800s to the mid-1900s. Given all that information, the winner is a bit of a shocker: a ref. 2215 from 1976 that exemplifies the qualities of the line but modernizes them in many ways. It doesn’t even feature a full set of numerals, trading them out for a few diamond-set indices. In his acceptance speech, the owner said he wears it on the weekends with jeans.

The Astronomical Complications category is dear to the heart of anyone who appreciates a good moonphase display and also includes timepieces equipped with a triple-calendar, a complete calendar, or a perpetual calendar. Though more modern pieces, such as a skeletonized QP wristwatch from 1987, made it to the final round, it was a wildly neat (and unique) platinum-cased “Cioccolatone” from 1957 that won out. Housed in a 34mm x 43mm rectangular case and equipped with a complete calendar, it’s owned by a dapper Italian collector, who beamed as he collected the prize with his grown son. This would not be this pair’s first time at the podium…

This is a loaded category for Vacheron, which famously makes the most complicated pocket watch and wristwatch in the world, with 57 and 41 complications, respectively. To be eligible in this category, watches were required to have at least two complications—child’s play for VC.

Spanning everything from an enamel-dialed, minute-repeating, split-seconds chronograph pocket watch from 1901 to several Patrimony watches from the 1990s, the winner was the “Don Pancho.” Delivered in 1940, this diminutive yellow-gold timepiece with minute repeater, day, and retrograde date indications was once the world’s most complicated wristwatch. Double-signed by Brooking in Madrid, it sold for roughly $740,000 at auction back in 2019.

A more subjective category, perhaps, than the others, Design included watches “featuring Vacheron Constantin’s signature design, either in the case or through the time display.” One entrant, for example—a wild time-only ref. 4695 dress watch—featured incredibly intricate lugs and a Maltese Cross-type dial. But the winner was nothing short of revelatory. Once again owned by the aforementioned tall Italian gentleman, the possibly unique ref. 6213 is an automatic world timer from 1957 in yellow gold. Based upon Louis Cottier’s famous system, it is so rare that even Clymer admitted he had never heard of it before the competition. The owner’s son described his father returning home with it one day when he was a boy, excited beyond belief that he had finally tracked it down after years of searching.

This category included pocket watches or wristwatches fitted with a minute repeater, quarter repeater, half-quarter repeater, or grand sonnerie—a mechanism that automatically strikes the hours and quarter-hours every 15 minutes. Incredibly, among the entrants was a red gold quarter-repeater pocket watch from the early 1820s with a stunning guilloché dial. However, the winner was another pocket watch dating to 1926 and cased in platinum. Its ultra-thin design, black Breguet numerals, Breguet blued steel handset, and simple silver dial belied the complex mechanism within. The visibly emotional American gentleman who owns it recalled how, as a boy, he would open a chest of drawers, remove his grandfather’s pocket watch, and listen to its minute repeater.

A bonus category, Best of Show went to a truly spectacular wristwatch: a ref. 6448 in platinum with diamond-set indices. Seemingly a simple time-only dress watch, this tremendous piece—which was produced in just three examples in the early 1960s—boasts a hand-wound, 13-ligne minute-repeater movement. Housed in a brushed-finish case with incredible teardrop lugs, it’s the only known example in this metal, and it was notably the last minute-repeating reference produced by the brand for nearly 30 years.

Nominally, the crowd at the awards ceremony was there to judge the merits of a watch, but I left emotionally moved by the stories each watch owner shared about their timepieces. As the very first concours for watches, the format will no doubt be repeated in the future—either by Vacheron, adopted by other brands, or done as a more traditional multi-brand event like the Concours d’Élégance at Pebble Beach.

#6677. Truman Capote’s Zoo, From a 1976 Issue of Vogue

Editor’s Note: Looking through the archive it feels like Truman Capote was almost as much in Vogue as he was hobnobbing with his society swans. It’s not surprising to learn that the author of Breakfast at Tiffany’s had a taste for the finer things in life. Some of Capote’s possessions will be sold by Cornell Auctions on November 21. A number of the lots appeared in a 1976 Vogue article, written by Leo Lerman, a virtual tour of “Capote’s Zoo.” Printed in black-and-white in the magazine, we are able to share color pictures of these figurines, and a few that didn’t make the edit.—LBP

“Capote’s Zoo,” by Leo Lerman with photographs by Horst P. Horst, was originally published in the July 1976 issue of Vogue.

Truman’s beasts, 24 of them, complete with Trumanisms, comments on his quarries by their see-all, tell-all keeper.... Three years ago, when Horst took this photograph [seen above], Truman Capote was smiling his I-know-a-secret smile. Now he’s still smiling—but it’s his come-little-ghostie-sit-on-my- knee smile—at the brouhaha over the cliff-hanger publication of his novel Answered Prayers (most recent chapter: “Unspoiled Monsters”), a book about the humans in his zoo.

It’s no secret that Truman Capote—Little T. to those who love him, The Tiny Terror to those who hate-love him—is passionate about secrets: his own, other people’s. His books are rife with them, brought to horrendous or hilarious or exquisite flower. The star-y role he plays in Neil Simon’s movie, Murder by Death, explodes with secrets. And in his apartment and three houses (Manhattan, Long Island, California, Switzerland), Truman has accumulated hundreds of objects—a zoo of beasts, many of which conceal secret repositories—little drawers, infinitesimal hollows.

“I’ve just been collecting for thousands of years,” says Little T.—his speaking voice ranges at least three octaves per sentence, from Little Nell to Old Mischief.  “And I bought all of these animals. I’ve collected them—well, all over the world. Why animals? I love animals per se, in real life.” Maggie, the presiding “real” beast, is a sedately rampageous, hideously attractive English bull, referred to by Capote as “my little doggie.” Little T. continues, “And I like objects, ’specially objects  that are—well, I don’t like them just for themselves. Usually I like them to be something else other than what they are. Like that English dog’s head over there with that cap on his head [Truman sometimes wears one very like it]—he’s one of my favorites, and he’s a tobacco jar. My house at the beach’s got just loads of marvelous, curious objects.”

And that’s what Truman Capote’s Zoo is all about: “marvelous, curious objects,” collected seriously for years—the inanimates like the ones on these pages, the animates in his writings from “Miriam” to Other Voices, Other Rooms to In Cold Blood to Answered Prayers—with its gamy-rich, pants-down fill of look-look-now, isn’t that Lady Κ., B.P., Princess R., T.W.? Isn’t that Little T. just loving them all to death for posterity? ... Little T. smiles seraphically, as he contemplates his zoo, peering at a life-sized, carved wooden tree about whose branches winds a terrifying wooden serpent. “That,” he murmurs sweetly, “came off a Zen temple.”

Below, 24 residents of the Manhattan Branch of Truman Capote’s Zoo, complete with Trumanisms about his creatures.

“It’s yellow, blue, and porcelain all over—this English, Victorian, last-laugh cat.”

“This Russian frog changes into a box.” Even frogs work in Russia.

“An English frog toting an inkwell.” Pumping iron? Even frogs are doing it at T.’s.

“It’s a children’s toy, a wooden, green, rocking parrot that Quakers carved long, long ago.”

“This Japanese ceramic cat is, I believe, seventeenth century.” A seraphic smiler.

“A perfect giraffe—silver, Portuguese....” He’s not a box—just an elegant observer.

“Two Meissen fowls fornicating.” That’s Capote telling it as it is in his zoo.

“I use these Chinese bronze rats as candle holders.” On his dining table, they’re right.

“And this is a Meissen rabbit—German, of course.” A haughty, businesslike bunny.

“What’s blue, white, porcelain all over? This Japanese, eighteenth-century creepy cat.”

“This owl is silver, Italian, eighteenth century....” And won’t talk—even for a mouse.

“This is a Japanese gold chipmunk.” Chipmunks must be different in Japan. Note ears.

“This green thing is Chinese porcelain. And its head moves!” Could be cat, pug?

“A white, horned English porcelain owl. The top opens up—the owl’s a tobacco jar.”

“This Eskimo-carved walrus is actually a box—its interior carved from walrus tusk.”

“One of my favorites, an English tobacco box.” Doggie’s sporting Truman’s hat.

“Japanese fishermen used these to ward off evil spirits.” Answered Prayers can try.

“Hand-carved, ivory Chinese boxes. Fat birds. And they open up!” T. loves that.

“Such a favorite, this Japanese rabbit baying at the moon.” Baying? Only for Little T.

“A tiny, Meissen parrot’s-head box. You open the head....” To find a Tiny Terror secret?

#6676. Léa Seydoux Isn’t Trying to Act. She’s Trying to Live

The French actress continues her string of emotionally demanding roles in The Unknown and Gentle Monster

Léa Seydoux first stepped into the limelight in Christophe Honoré’s The Beautiful Person, where her role as Junie de Chartres earned her the Trophée Chopard award for rising actors at Cannes. From there, she moved seamlessly between highbrow French cinema and Hollywood, achieving a critical breakthrough with Blue Is the Warmest Color in 2013 and starring alongside Daniel Craig as a Bond girl in Spectre and No Time to Die. Most years, she’s starred in at least two films, and 2026 is no exception: She plays a woman with a man’s soul trapped in her body in Arthur Harari’s psychological fantasy The Unknown, and in Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster, releasing on Netflix on November 18, she’s a pianist who unearths her husband’s hideous crimes. The words thorny and barbed read like understatements for both films, and it’s exactly what interests Seydoux about the stories. Like in life itself, she avoids easy answers, opting instead for exploration.

Seydoux got the chance to explore an especially ambitious idea in The Unknown. It tells the story of David Zimmerman (Niels Schneider), a photographer who wakes up in the body of a woman he sleeps with. Seydoux plays both that woman, Eva, and the man trapped within her body. “I felt the movie was something new to me, to play an impossible idea and make it believable, try to give it a truthful dimension,” Seydoux says. She’s no stranger to high-concept stories, previously starring in Bertrand Bonello’s The Beast and David Cronenberg’s Crimes of the Future. Each time, she imbues these characters with humanity, despite their far-fetched sci-fi dilemmas.

“I like movies that make you think, movies that bring up questions, when there’s a debate around the film,” she says. “What I love the most is to explore human nature, our human condition. This is what cinema allows us to do.”

Seydoux might vehemently love movies, yet acting remains a demanding process for her. She relies on the art form to dig into feelings and emotions. “I don’t feel necessarily very comfortable with acting. It’s not a place where I’m like, ‘I love it,’ but at the same time, I find it a bit painful. It’s more a way to experience things and ideas,” she says.

Gentle Monster provides another knotty premise, this time grounded in reality. It follows Lucy Weiss, a famed experimental pianist who gives up her career to raise her young son with her doting husband, Philip (Laurence Rupp). One day, the police knock on their door, and it’s revealed that Philip is accused of distributing child pornography.

“The subject matter is tough, but the fact that it’s through the woman’s perspective—and not through the victim or perpetrator—it’s through her emotions that the story unfolds [is what interested me],” she says. “Things are not too defined, but it’s also because of the subject matter; it was the only way to talk about it. [Marie] gave me a lot of freedom.”

Born in Paris in 1985, Seydoux spent her childhood wedged among seven siblings and half-siblings. She remembers feeling isolated, practically invisible, as a child. “I was always in the shadows in a way,” she says. “As a kid, I felt transparent. I was never at the center of [my] big family.” This plays a big part in her surprise at her acting career, never thinking of herself as someone deserving of center stage, of fame, of attention. In fact, acting never even crossed her mind until she befriended some actors when she turned 18. “I loved the way they lived their lives,” she says. “I admired their life—the fact that they were free.”

And yet, she rejects the label of “actress.” “I try to be truthful as much as possible,” she says. “I try not to act. This is what I try to be, and I’m more into reaction than action.” She adds, “It’s more reactive than acting.”

For Seydoux, “reacting” and really experiencing life is only possible if she “abandons” herself to her characters. One of the most intense examples of this is Abdellatif Kechiche’s controversial lesbian love story Blue Is the Warmest Color, in which she stars alongside Adèle Exarchopoulos. The film’s schedule stretched from two months to five months, and it has since become notorious for its grueling pace. (The famous sex scene took 10 days alone.) “The greatest and most intense experience I’ve had was with Adèle when we did Blue Is the Warmest Color,” she recalls. “It was crazy, and really the connection between us had to be very, very intense. I think, with Adèle, it’s something that will always be a part of me now. There was an exchange, and it was more than making a film. It was really a life experience.”

One scene from Gentle Monster lingered with me for weeks after I watched it: Lucy’s snotty, tearful confrontation with her husband at their family home as she pleads with him to tell the truth. This close-up of Seydoux not only accentuates her famous blue eyes but also shows her uncanny control of this character’s emotions. It feels, for lack of better words, real. Seydoux partly credits her empathy to being a mother of two children, but this scene goes beyond compassion; it shows how much of herself she gives to the character. Before filming this scene, Kreutzer offered little direction, letting her tap into how the character felt. “I prepare myself, and I have to just let myself go and be in the moment and just open up,” Seydoux says, suggesting that perhaps these emotions otherwise lie dormant within her.

I found this is what Seydoux means by “reaction.” Every role in her varied and extolled filmography functions as an avenue through which she can explore what it means to be human, what it means to feel. Her natural curiosity about the world and its inhabitants existed before she decided to act in her teens and will exist long into the future, even if acting jobs don’t remain on the table. “If it ended tomorrow, I’d be happy,” she says. “I will find a way. Now, I really feel that I’m acting because I still have the opportunity. But I have more things to explore, and I would love to have more experiences.”

In a world where we’re hunched over our computers from nine to five, and then slouched and scrolling from five to nine, good posture is a rarity. But that doesn’t mean we should just accept a fate of poor spinal alignment. Especially when there’s actually a really easy solution (that doesn’t include deleting TikTok from your iPhone).

Allow me to introduce you to the posture-correcting bra. Along with delivering superior support, the shapewear category uses stretchy fabrics with varying levels of tension to reposition your shoulders and help you breathe better. Taylor Swift even wore one while training for the Eras Tour—and hers alone is low-key life-changing.

Now, even the best posture bras aren't intended to fix serious medical issues on their own, so it's not a substitute for, say, a scoliosis brace. But if you're looking for a little extra help retraining your body to sit up straight with your head held high, these types of bras encourage small corrections in the right direction!

A posture-correcting bra works best alongside an ergonomic chair, Pilates classes, or a new mattress, rather than as a replacement for any of them. It also happens to be the smallest investment of the bunch, and editors like me are big fans. Keep reading for my top picks—including the one and only Taylor Swift-approved option.

#6674. Black Doves Adds Your Favorite ’90s Scream Queen to Season 2—Meet the New and Returning Cast

It features Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw, and Neve Campbell.

Black Doves is back, and it’s just as action-packed as ever. Netflix’s deadly, dark, and irreverently funny spy thriller follows a covert intelligence organization as it uncovers and sells secrets among the rich and powerful. Season 1 brought us Keira Knightley as the fearless agent Helen; Sarah Lancashire as her icy spymaster, Reed; and Ben Whishaw as an assassin and Helen’s longtime friend.

That first season closed with many loose ends, so it wasn’t a huge surprise when it was announced that we’d be seeing Helen and Sam in action again. Now, season 2 has brought the pair back to our screens, with a handful of fresh faces to add to the drama. This time around, Sam appears as a washed-up hit man taking low-paid jobs, while Helen is still working for the Black Doves—something that proves to be complicated given her husband, Wallace (played by Andrew Buchan), is now prime minister.

All episodes of the new season dropped on Netflix on November 5. If you’re eager to get to know the cast and characters more closely—and are wondering where you might have seen those new faces before—then read on.

As an agent of the Black Doves, Helen Webb is tasked with gathering highly sensitive information obtained via her politician husband, Wallace. But keeping up the image of a good spouse, mother, and spy all at once becomes increasingly difficult to maintain, and Helen grows conflicted about her life of betrayal. You’ll know Keira Knightley, of course, from her career of starry roles in everything from Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean to Pride & Prejudice, Bend It Like Beckham, and Love Actually.

Helen’s close friend, a previously high-flying hit man, an ex-employee of the Black Doves, Sam Young attempted to leave behind his former life—but that was easier said than done. Now he’s taking low-paid jobs and drinking alone in bars, before he finds himself roped into business with Helen once again. You’ll know Whishaw from his role in Daniel Craig’s James Bond films—Skyfall, Spectre, and No Time to Die—as well as A Very English Scandal and The Hour.

Relentless and cold, the spymaster Reed is Helen’s handler at the Black Doves and does not mess around. In season 2, we see new, more vulnerable sides of her character unfold via glimpses of her younger self and flashes to the past events that came to define her. You’ll recognize Lancashire from her role in Happy Valley.

Wallace Webb is Helen’s husband and the father of her two children, and he’s completely unaware of her career as a Black Dove. In season 2, his own career has taken off and he becomes the U.K.’s prime minister—a move that comes with highly strict security measures in the backdrop of rising tensions in his marriage. Buchan has also starred in Industry, The Crown, and Carnival Row.

Another assassin, Williams, worked for the crime leader Lenny in the first season of Black Doves. This time around, she’s moved on and formed a partnership with Eleanor, following the death of her previous partner, as well as a friendship with Sam. Hyland has starred in Towards Zero, A Thousand Blows, and Tall Tales and Murder.

As Williams’s partner, Eleanor is another fast-footed assassin with a refreshing sense of humor. Creevy has also starred in Amadeus, The Guest, and Operation Mincemeat.

Laila is an assassin with a fun, nonchalant, and lighthearted personality—a contrast to Helen, whom she clashes with at the start of season 2. You’ll know Ambika Mod for her roles in This Is Going to Hurt and as the co-lead of Netflix’s One Day adaptation.

Mr. Conteh is a senior at Black Doves and is hungry for power. As the fabric of the institution is put under pressure and he is sent to investigate Reed, Conteh becomes increasingly prominent for Helen and her associates. Ceesay has also starred in Alien: Earth.

Cruelly minded and understated in tone, Patrick works for a rival organization to Black Doves, the same group that presents an appealing get-out for Sam when he needs it the most. Riley also starred in the comedy-horror Pride and Prejudice and Zombies as well as Firebrand.

Hard-headed with tunnel vision, Cecile Mason is a U.S. defense envoy, arriving at 10 Downing Street to work on relations between the president and the prime minister ahead of a major peace summit. Campbell was a star of the Scream movies, as well as Party of Five and Wild Things.

Glamorous and sharp-minded, Katia Chernov is the wife of Russian oligarch Alexi Chernov and becomes swept up in the mysteries in the new series. She’s played by Sylvia Hoeks, who has also starred in Blade Runner 2049 and The Girl in the Spider’s Web.

A well-connected Russian oligarch with immeasurable influence and power, Alexi Chernov is a force to be reckoned with in season 2, with fingers in some of the most fragile cases. He’s played by Goran Kostić, whom you may recognize from Ant-Man and the Wasp or Canary Black.

#6673. Christy Turlington’s Ruby-Red Lipstick Is the Easy Makeup Secret for Women Over 40

Shop our favorite creamy, hydrating, and smoothing lipstick formulas

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The last few years have been marked by the “Lip Balm Wars.” That is, every brand—from Hailey Bieber’s Rhode to prestige labels like Chanel and Dior—has launched more sheer, glossy, and hydrating formulas than classic lipstick bullets. But even though we all own more than 10 emotional-support lip balms in various shades, flavors, and finishes, there's still nothing more powerful than a statement-making lip. This is especially true for women over 40.

Last night, supermodel Christy Turlington stepped out at the Museum of Modern Art’s 2026 Annual Film Benefit in New York, wearing a knit dress from Matthieu Blazy’s fall 2026 Chanel collection. A dress this graphic and eye-catching needs makeup to balance it, and Turlington paired it with black eyeliner and a glossy ruby-red lipstick.

While we don’t know the exact shade she wore last night, it’s clearly a formula that sits somewhere between a satin lipstick and a gloss-balm, with pigment that doesn’t sacrifice moisture or shine. Turlington is a Lancôme ambassador, so it could be the brand’s Lip Idole Butterglow Hydrating Lip Balm or L’Absolu Rouge Cream Lipstick. Otherwise, Chanel makes a gorgeous option in both the Rouge Coco Flash and Rouge Allure Extrait formulas. These formulas subtly plump and moisturize dry lips while blurring lip lines and imperfections.

Lancôme L'Absolu Rouge Moisturizing Cream Lipstick in 397 Berry Noir

Chanel Hydrating Vibrant Shine Lip Colour

Lancome Lip Idole Squalane-12 Butterglow Hydrating Lip Balm

The best part of this look is that it proves you don’t need to match your lipstick exactly to your outfit, as long as they’re in the same color family. While the Chanel dress is more of an orange-red knit, Turlington’s lipstick is a more neutral ruby that harmonizes with the warm tones and shades in the rest of her look. Plus, raspberry or ruby-red lipstick can brighten your face in seconds, even with little to no other makeup.

Bold lipstick is a bit outside Turlington’s day-to-day comfort zone; she told Bazaar recently that she’s “definitely an old-school Carmex or ChapStick kind of person, because I’m constantly reapplying it to my dry lips, especially in the winter.” The rest of her routine is equally as effortless: “I wash my face in the morning and moisturize a lot. Sometimes I even double-moisturize because, especially at this time of year, I get dry skin. And then, I’ll add a nice little layer of foundation, some blush, and mascara, and that’s kind of it, I’m on my way.”
